questions.question: How does a DataFrame differ from a two-dimensional NumPy array?
options: A DataFrame can only hold numbers, while a NumPy array can hold text as well.
A DataFrame has labelled rows and columns and allows a different dtype in each column.
A DataFrame is always one-dimensional internally and only displays itself as a table.
A DataFrame stores every column as one shared dtype so that sums are always exact.
questions.explanation: A DataFrame is a table of Series that share a row index; each column keeps its own dtype, so text, integers, and floats can sit side by side. A NumPy array has one dtype for all cells and no labels.
questions.misconception: Mixed dtypes per column is the DataFrame's key difference from a 2D array.

questions.question: What do `films["lead"]` and `films[["lead"]]` return?
options: Both return a Series, because each call names a single column.
A DataFrame for the first and a Series for the second, because a list always adds a dimension.
A Series for the first and a one-column DataFrame for the second, because a list selects a DataFrame.
Both return a DataFrame, because square brackets on a DataFrame always return a table.
questions.explanation: A single name returns a Series; a list of names returns a DataFrame, even when the list has one item. This matters when later code expects a table or a column.
questions.misconception: The brackets inside the brackets change the result type.

questions.scenario: A DataFrame is indexed by names `["ada", "bo", "cal", "dee", "eli"]`. You want rows from `bo` through `dee`, including `dee`.
questions.question: Which expression does that?
options: `df.iloc["bo":"dee"]`, because slices on names work with position-based access.
`df.loc["bo":"dee"]`, because label slices with `loc` include the end label.
`df.loc[1:3]`, because `loc` accepts positions when the index holds strings.
`df.iloc[1:3]`, because the end position is included just as it is for labels.
questions.explanation: `loc` selects by label and includes the end label, so it returns bo, cal, and dee. `iloc` takes integer positions only, and its end is excluded, so `iloc[1:3]` would stop before `dee`.

questions.question: Why does `m[(m["Season"] == "2015") and (m["City"] == "Kolkata")]` raise a `ValueError`?
options: Because `Season` holds strings, and strings cannot be compared with `==` inside a DataFrame filter.
Because the filter needs a third condition, since two conditions cannot be combined by a single operator.
Because `and` tries to reduce a whole Series to one `True` or `False`; use `&` with parentheses instead.
Because DataFrames cannot be filtered by two columns at once, only by a single column.
questions.explanation: Python's `and` needs a single truth value, which a Series does not have. The bitwise `&` works element by element, and each condition needs parentheses because `&` binds more tightly than `==`.
questions.misconception: Use `&`, `|`, and `~` for element-wise logic on Series.

questions.question: For a table of students (rows) and subjects (columns), what does `marks.mean(axis=1)` give?
options: One average per subject, computed down each column.
One average per student, computed across that student's subjects.
A single number, the average of every cell in the table.
A table of the same shape, with each cell replaced by its row average.
questions.explanation: Axis 1 runs across the columns, so each row collapses to one value: a per-student average. Axis 0, the default, runs down the rows and gives a per-subject result.
questions.misconception: `axis=1` reduces across a row; the default `axis=0` reduces down a column.

questions.scenario: You filter a match table with `dl = m[m["method"] == "D/L"]` and want to know how many matches qualify.
questions.question: Which expression answers that?
options: `dl.shape[0]`, because `shape` is rows then columns and the first value is the row count.
`dl.shape[1]`, because the second value of `shape` counts the matching records.
`dl.values`, because the number of values equals the number of matches.
`dl.dtypes`, because it reports one entry per matching row.
questions.explanation: `shape` is `(rows, columns)`, so `shape[0]` is the number of rows. `shape[1]` is the number of columns, `values` returns the data itself, and `dtypes` lists one dtype per column.

questions.question: Among toss winners who chose to field, you compute `(sub["TossWinner"] == sub["WinningTeam"]).mean()` and get 0.55. What does that number mean?
options: 55 percent of all matches in the file were won by the team that fielded first.
The toss winner's name matches the winner's name in 55 rows, a raw count.
55 percent of the fielding toss winners in this subset also won the match.
The toss decision caused the win in 55 percent of matches, so fielding is the better choice.
questions.explanation: The comparison gives a boolean per row, and the mean of booleans is the share of `True`. It applies to the subset of fielding toss winners, in this sample. It is a count only if you use `sum`, and it does not show causation.
questions.misconception: A share in a subset describes association in the sample, not cause.

questions.question: The `genres` column holds text like `"Mystery, Musical"`. How do you keep every film that lists Comedy anywhere in that text?
options: `films[films["genres"] == "Comedy"]`, because equality finds the word inside longer text.
`films[films["genres"].str.contains("Comedy")]`, because it tests for a substring in each value.
`films[films["genres"].isin("Comedy")]`, because `isin` looks for a word inside each string.
`films.loc["Comedy"]`, because `loc` can search the text of every column.
questions.explanation: `==` matches only entire values, so films listing several genres would be missed. `str.contains` checks for a substring. `isin` expects a list of whole values, and `loc` selects by row label.
questions.misconception: Equality tests the whole cell; `str.contains` tests part of it.

questions.scenario: You build `df["first"] = df["genres"].str.split(", ").apply(lambda p: p[0])`, but the column contains missing values and the call fails.
questions.question: What is the sound fix?
options: Convert the whole table with `astype("int32")`, which removes missing values.
Sort the DataFrame by `genres` first, which moves the missing values out of the way.
Use `iloc` instead, because positional access ignores missing values.
Drop or fill the missing values first, for example with `dropna(subset=["genres"])`.
questions.explanation: A missing value is a float `NaN`, which has no `split` result to index. Remove or fill those rows before applying the function. Sorting only moves them, `astype` to an integer type would fail on missing values, and `iloc` does not change the data.
questions.misconception: Row-by-row functions break on `NaN` unless it is handled first.

questions.question: What does `df.insert(1, "decade", values)` do that `df["decade"] = values` does not?
options: It places the new column at position 1 instead of at the end.
It copies the DataFrame first, so the original table stays untouched.
It allows values of a different length than the table, padding with missing values.
It sorts the columns alphabetically after adding the new one.
questions.explanation: `insert` chooses the position of the new column. It changes the DataFrame in place and returns `None`, requires matching length, and does not reorder other columns.
questions.misconception: Assignment always appends; only `insert` sets the position.

questions.question: Why does converting `Venue` to the `category` dtype shrink memory so much in the match table?
options: It deletes the rows with repeated venue names, keeping one row per venue.
It stores each venue name as a float, which needs fewer bytes than text.
It truncates every venue name to a fixed short length.
It stores each distinct name once and keeps a small integer code per row.
questions.explanation: Text that repeats is stored once in a lookup of categories, and each row holds a compact code. No rows are removed, names are not truncated, and floats do not shrink text.
questions.misconception: Category saves memory through codes, not by dropping data.

questions.question: What dtype does `films.values` have for a table with text and numeric columns?
options: `int64`, because the numeric columns take priority over the text.
`object`, because one NumPy array must hold a single type that fits every column.
`float64`, because pandas converts text to numbers when building the array.
A separate dtype for each column, because NumPy supports mixed columns.
questions.explanation: `values` returns one NumPy array. With mixed columns the only common type is `object`. Per-column dtypes live on the DataFrame (`dtypes`), not on the array.
questions.misconception: Column dtypes are a DataFrame feature; the plain array loses them.

questions.scenario: You load an unfamiliar table and want to see which columns have missing values and what each dtype is.
questions.question: Which call gives that overview in one step?
options: `describe()`, because it lists non-null counts and dtypes for every column.
`head()`, because the first rows show every missing value in the table.
`info()`, because it prints non-null counts, dtypes, and memory use per column.
`rename()`, because it reports the labels that need to be changed.
questions.explanation: `info()` reports non-null counts, dtypes, and memory. `describe()` summarizes numeric columns with statistics, `head()` shows only a few rows, and `rename()` relabels.

questions.question: Explain the difference between `loc` and `iloc`, including how each treats the end of a slice.
questions.answer: `iloc` selects by integer position and excludes the end of a slice, like a Python list. `loc` selects by row or column label and includes the end label. Both take a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma.
questions.explanation: When the index is the default 0, 1, 2, and so on, the two look alike, but the end rule still differs.
